title: 10. Exercises: 19 — 15 Coding Challenges (No Answers)
summary: Time-box yourself: 30–45 minutes per challenge. Write tests for each.
objectives: Solve the 19 — 15 Coding Challenges (No Answers) exercises without looking at the lesson
Test edge cases and explain your approach

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Time-box yourself: 30–45 minutes per challenge. Write tests for each. After your attempt, look up the canonical solution and compare.

For each problem, before coding, write down:

1. **Inputs / outputs** (with types and ranges).
2. **Edge cases** (empty, one element, duplicates, negatives, huge input).
3. **Approach** (data structure + algorithm) and complexity.
4. **Then** code.

sections.title: Challenge 1 — Word Frequency in a Huge Log
sections.body:
**Scenario.** You are given a 5 GB text file `access.log`. Each line contains plain text. Write a Python program that prints the top 10 most frequent words (case-insensitive, ignoring punctuation) along with their counts. The machine has 4 GB RAM.

**Constraints / cover:** file streaming, generators, `collections.Counter`, regex, memory-efficient design.

sections.title: Challenge 2 — CSV → JSON Transformer with Validation
sections.body:
**Scenario.** Build a CLI tool: `python tool.py users.csv users.json`.

- CSV columns: `id, name, email, age, joined_at`.
- Validate: `id` is int, `email` matches RFC-ish regex, `age` 0–150, `joined_at` is ISO date.
- Bad rows go to `errors.csv` with a reason column. Good rows go to JSON array.
- Use Pydantic for validation.

**Cover:** file handling, CSV, JSON, Pydantic, exceptions, CLI (`argparse`).

sections.title: Challenge 3 — Concurrent URL Health Checker
sections.body:
**Scenario.** Given a list of 1,000 URLs, fetch each, capture status code + response time. Output a summary CSV. Implement two versions:

1. Using `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor`.
2. Using `asyncio` + `aiohttp`.

Compare runtimes. Limit concurrency to 50.

**Cover:** threading, async, semaphores, timeouts, error handling.

sections.title: Challenge 4 — LRU Cache from Scratch
sections.body:
**Scenario.** Implement `class LRUCache` supporting `get(key)` and `put(key, value)` in O(1) average. Capacity given in constructor; evict least-recently-used on overflow. Do **not** use `functools.lru_cache` or `OrderedDict` — build it with a dict + doubly linked list.

**Cover:** DSA, OOP, dunder methods (`__len__`, `__contains__`).

sections.title: Challenge 5 — Producer / Consumer Pipeline
sections.body:
**Scenario.** One producer reads numbers from `numbers.txt` (one per line). Three consumers compute `n*n` and write `(n, square)` to `squares.csv` in any order. Use a bounded queue (max size 100) for backpressure. Graceful shutdown when producer is done.

**Cover:** threading, `queue.Queue`, sentinel/poison-pill pattern, file IO.

sections.title: Challenge 6 — Custom Context Manager: chdir
sections.body:
**Scenario.** Implement `with chdir(path):` that changes CWD on enter and restores it on exit, even if the inside block raises. Provide both class-based and `@contextmanager` versions. Add tests proving the CWD is restored on exception.

**Cover:** context managers, `os`, exceptions, testing.

sections.title: Challenge 7 — Mini ORM with Descriptors & Metaclass
sections.body:
**Scenario.** Build a tiny ORM:

```python
class User(Model):
    id = IntField(primary=True)
    name = StringField(max_length=50)
    age = IntField(min=0, max=150)
```

- Field descriptors validate on assignment.
- A metaclass collects fields and registers the model.
- `User.objects.all()` returns instances loaded from an in-memory dict (no real DB).
- `user.save()` persists to that dict.

**Cover:** OOP deep, metaclasses, descriptors, dunder methods.

sections.title: Challenge 8 — Streaming Top-K
sections.body:
**Scenario.** Implement a `TopK(k)` class that consumes an unbounded stream of (key, score) updates and at any time returns the current top K keys by latest score in O(log n) per update. Updates may overwrite existing keys' scores.

**Cover:** heaps, dicts, lazy deletion, OOP.

sections.title: Challenge 9 — Word Count MapReduce-style
sections.body:
**Scenario.** Split a 1 GB text into N chunks, count words per chunk in parallel using `multiprocessing.Pool`, then merge into a single `Counter`. Compare wall time vs single-process. Verify total counts match.

**Cover:** multiprocessing, GIL bypass, chunking, `Counter` merge.

sections.title: Challenge 10 — Retry Decorator with Backoff
sections.body:
**Scenario.** Build `@retry(attempts=3, backoff=0.5, exceptions=(ConnectionError,))` that retries the wrapped function on listed exceptions, doubling the delay each time, and re-raises after attempts are exhausted. Preserve the wrapped function's name/doc. Make it usable on both sync and async functions.

**Cover:** decorators, async, exception handling, `functools.wraps`.

sections.title: Challenge 11 — JSON Diff Tool
sections.body:
**Scenario.** Given two JSON files `a.json` and `b.json` (arbitrary nested), print all differences in dotted path form:

```
users[2].email: "a@x" -> "a@y"
config.timeout: <missing> -> 30
items[5]: <removed>
```

Support nested objects, arrays, type changes.

**Cover:** recursion, JSON, strings, edge cases.

sections.title: Challenge 12 — Generator Pipeline for ETL
sections.body:
**Scenario.** Read `transactions.csv` (id, user_id, amount, status). Build a generator pipeline:

1. parse → `dict`
2. filter `status == "completed"`
3. enrich with user name from `users.csv` (loaded into dict once)
4. group by user_id and yield `(user_id, total_amount)` once input ends.

Constraints: never load the full transactions file into memory.

**Cover:** generators, comprehensions, file IO, `defaultdict`, `itertools.groupby`.

sections.title: Challenge 13 — Thread-safe Singleton with Double-Checked Locking
sections.body:
**Scenario.** Implement a `Config` singleton class such that:

- Only one instance exists app-wide.
- It is safe under concurrent `Config()` calls from many threads.
- Expensive `_load()` method runs at most once.

Then critique your own design: would a module-level instance be better?

**Cover:** OOP, `__new__`, threading locks, design discussion.

sections.title: Challenge 14 — Data Validation Library (No Pydantic)
sections.body:
**Scenario.** Build a tiny `Schema` system:

```python
schema = Schema({
    "name": Str(min_len=1, max_len=50),
    "age": Int(min=0, max=150),
    "tags": List(Str()),
    "address": Schema({"city": Str()}),
})
schema.validate(data)   # returns cleaned data or raises ValidationError
```

Errors must include the dotted path: `address.city: required`.

**Cover:** OOP, recursion, exceptions, design principles, `__call__` optional.

sections.title: Challenge 15 — Mini Async Web Crawler
sections.body:
**Scenario.** Given a starting URL and a max depth, asynchronously crawl pages on the same domain, collect every `<a href>` link, and write a `sitemap.json` mapping URL → list of links. Concurrency limited to 20 requests at a time. Skip already-visited URLs. Respect a 5-second per-request timeout.

**Cover:** asyncio, semaphores, sets, exception handling, parsing (regex or BeautifulSoup).

sections.title: Final advice for the interview
sections.body:
1. **Talk while coding.** State assumptions, edge cases, complexity _before_ typing.
2. **Start brute force, then optimize.** Better to finish O(n²) than half-write O(n log n).
3. **Always handle edge cases**: empty, single, duplicates, negatives, overflow, None.
4. **Name things well**, even in interviews. Clean code signals seniority.
5. **Test mentally** with one tiny input before declaring done.
6. **If stuck**, restate the problem; the interviewer will often nudge you.
7. **For concept questions**, use the **C-S-E-T** template (Concept, Syntax, Example, Tradeoff).

You will crack it. Practice each topic + 20 questions + the 15 challenges, and the interview becomes routine.
